kandidaty.zagolovok: Claude Platform release notes — November 9, 2026
kandidaty.tekst:
- We’ve launched Claude Fable 5.2 (claude-fable-5-2), built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work. Claude Mythos 5.2 (claude-mythos-5-2) offers the same capabilities only to organizations verified through Anthropic’s verification programs, such as the Cyber Verification Program. Both models have a 1M token context window, 128k max output tokens, and always-on adaptive thinking. They cost $8 USD per MTok of input and $40 USD per MTok of output (Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 cost $10 USD per MTok of input and $50 USD per MTok of output). Claude Fable 5.2 is available on the Claude API, Amazon Bedrock (bedrock-runtime), Claude Platform on AWS, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed), Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed), and Claude in Microsoft Foundry. See What’s new in Claude Fable 5.2 for API changes and migration guidance. For model-specific prompting patterns, see Prompting Claude Fable 5.2.

- Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 enforce the prefix check for every account, whatever its age. Claude Fable 5.1 returns the error by default on accounts created on or after August 31, 2026 (see When prefix_mismatch_behavior is unset). If your code edits the system prompt, tools, or an earlier message and then sends back a Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 thinking block from a later turn, the request returns a 400 error. Before you switch, check whether your code edits the prefix.

- Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 read other models’ thinking blocks on the Claude API and Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed). So on those platforms, a conversation that moves onto either model keeps its reasoning. The other models include Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Haiku 5.5.

- No other model reads thinking blocks from Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2. When a conversation moves from either one to a model outside this pair, the API drops those blocks. That includes a move to Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Fable 5.1. The request still succeeds. See Switching models mid-conversation.

- Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 support computer use through the computer_toolset_20260801 toolset. A request that declares the earlier computer_20251124 tool returns a 400 error on every platform except Amazon Bedrock, where the earlier tool still works. See Migrate from computer_20251124.

- With the advisor tool, which is in beta, a Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 executor accepts only Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 as its advisor. Any other advisor returns a 400 error, so set the advisor’s model to one of these two models when you move an executor to them. Every executor model accepts Claude Fable 5.2 as its advisor. See Model compatibility.

- Both models require 30-day data retention, like Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. They aren’t available under zero data retention unless expressly authorized by Anthropic. See Model-specific data retention requirements.

Google Launches Gemini Decision 1 for Single-Pass Classification

Gemini Decisions API: Google introduced a new API backed by Gemini Decision 1. The model handles closed-set decisions, so it scores choices in a single pass instead of generating text token by token (Sundar Pichai, Logan Kilpatrick, Google).

Specs: It supports yes/no, multiple-choice and rubric scoring, with up to 255 multiple-choice options. It accepts text, image, audio, video and PDF inputs, handles up to 1,000 questions per request, has 256K context, returns answers in 150–250 ms end to end, and attaches a confidence score to every answer (@_philschmid).

Pricing: $0.10 per 1M input tokens, with $0 billed for output. Google says that is about 5x cheaper than Flash-Lite (Sundar).

Origin: The project started as an internal Google DeepMind prototype. A small team shipped the model and API about six weeks later (@_philschmid).

Google's comparison with TypeSafe's Jev: Google's own tests show Decision 1 beating Jev 1.14 on 5 of 7 shared benchmarks, including 92.2% vs 90.0% on JevBench. Jev costs $0.042 per 1M input tokens (@kimmonismus).

Artificial Analysis evaluation: Independent results are more mixed (Artificial Analysis).

aws-emulator

Finally, an official emulator from AWS to run tests against a local clone of their many different services without having to provision a paid API key to do so.

It's written in Rust by a huge swarm of agents - 29,684 commits in the first three weeks of the project. Swaminathan (Swami) Sivasubramanian wrote about how it came to be in a guest post on Werner Vogels' blog.

It currently requires Docker to run on macOS or Windows. I'm hoping they fix that in the future - it would be great if you could download a single binary and use that as part of a standard test suite in other languages and on other platforms.

kandidaty.zagolovok: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
kandidaty.tekst:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video

Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.

The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.

I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]

As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]

The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.

Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.

Tags: ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, gpus, claude-mythos-fable, recursive-self-improvement

Now I’m having fun!

My Ramp post was really well received with one or two ‘I’m not sure what I just looked at’ comments (which is totally fair).

The best I can describe what I’m doing now is exploring people and companies who are having fun with AI, doing things differently, being authentic and succeeding.

Which is basically how I want to describe my ‘work’.

But I think a lot of people are living in fear. Scared they’re behind, they’re not doing enough, others using AI ‘better’ than them, where’s there job going etc.

I want to focus on using AI for fun.

AI is a tool, you need one agent app (I’ve been using Droid with Opus 5.5 medium, fast mode for my posts, fable here and there). Use the tool to do work beyond what you could do before, don’t think about how you can finally optimise every aspect of every little thing. (I’ve basically stopped using Grok Bot, except telling me when the tennis is on).

As part of my explorations I’m working on a new post for another company I admire and who do things very differently. Coming next week…
